SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, there are two types of checks which are done, one is 
the pre-despatch inspection and the other is the quality audit. Quality audit is over and 
above the pre-despatch inspection. As the name implies, pre-despatch inspection is pre-
despatch. Quality audit is carried out after the items or the products have been received by 
the consumers, that is, the buyer. That is done as a precautionary measure over and above, 
as the word implies, it is 'quality audit'. So, pre-despatch inspection is one part of it. That 
having been done, in about six per cent of the cases, as a matter of abundant caution, and, 
in cases where the stores are large or the items can be manipulated in despatch, then a 
quality audit is done. So, as the hon. Member asked about the quality audit, my 
response is regarding quality audit. But I would like to inform him that quality audit 
supersedes, that is, over and above, the pre-despatch inspection.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
"Police" and "Public Order" are state subjects under the seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India and therefore the primary responsibility for detection, 
registration, investigation and prosecution as well as prevention of crime lies with the 
State Governments. lncluding crime committed on running trains. With a view to provide 
better security to the travelling passengers in trains and passenger areas, the 
Government has taken the following measures: 
(i) The Railway Protection Force Act, 1957 and the Railways Act, 1989 have 
been amended to enable the Railways, through the Railway Protection Force 
(RPF), to effectively control crime on railways in collaboration with State 
Police Force. 
(ii) RPF has also been empowered to deal with minor offences affecting the train 
operations such as alarm, chain pulling, roof travel, touting, ticket-less 
travelling, unauthorized entry. 
(iii) RPF personnel are being deployed to escort many trains and they are also 
being deployed in the passenger area. 
(iv) Coordination meetings between railways and state police are held periodically 
to reivew remedial measures for prevention of crimes on railways, the 
position in the sections, trains and stations affected by crimes. 
(v) Whenever there is a flare-up of violent incidents in any section, all-out efforts 
are made in coordination with the state police to control the situation, by 
actively assisting them with additional man power and other resources.

(a) According to the Wastelands Atlas of India, published in 2005 by the

(b) and (c) The aim of wasteland development is to improve degraded and 
wastelands through efficient adoption of the principles of restoration, 
conservation and ecological balance. Accordingly, the guidelines for the area 
development programmes of the Department of Land Resources have been 
formulated on the wasteland approach. The activities under these programmes 
include soil and moisture conservation works, harvesting of rain water, 
afforestation, horticulture, floriculture, development of pasture lands, fisheries, 
etc. to generate employment in the rural areas. To check overuse of natural 
resources and to ensure its efficient management, the schemes have adopted 
the participatory approach encourages village communities towards sustained 
community action for the maintenance of assets created and promotes simple,

under Entry No. 18 of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. State Governments 
distribute Government wastelands to the eligible landless rural poor. According 
to the reports received from the State Governments, an area of 147.47 lakh acres

Role of Coast Guard in protecting our fishermen 
3076. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Coast Guard has any responsibility to protect our fishermen and 
guide them in sensitive places near the border of other countries; 
(b) if so, what steps is the Coast Guard taking to give priority to ensure that our 
fishermen do not stray near or into the waters of any nearby country; 
(c) has the Coast Guard implemented any such task in the last year; 
(d) whether it is a fact that the Coast Guard has not lived upto the expectations in 
protecting and guiding our fishermen; and 
(e) steps proposed to review the functioning of our Coast Guard? 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) to (e) The 
Indian Coast Guard is entrusted with responsibility of maintaining round the clock 
surveillance in the Indian Exclusive Economic Zone and monitoring the operations of all the 
fishing vessels beyond the Territorial Waters of India. Therefore, protecting our 
fishermen and guiding them in the areas near the borders of other countries is an 
important task that is included in the Charter of Duties of the Indian Coast Guard. 
Indian fishermen are regularly advised to keep clear of the International Maritime 
Boundary Line by at least five nautical miles, to avoid interception and 
apprehension by the security forces of other countries. Community Interaction 
Programmes are also organized at frequent intervals along the coastal villages of our 
country where Coast Guard personnel educate our fishermen community not to 
cross the international Maritime Boundary Line. 
Differentiation between operation VIJAY and post-operation                                           
VIJAY casualties 
3077. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of 
DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government has drawn distinction between operation 
VIJAY and post operation VIJAY casualties thus diluting the benefits being extended 
by Government to the widows/NOKs of post operation VIJAY Battle casualties; 
and 
(b) if so, what steps Government propose to take to remove this anomaly which 
is not only against the natural justice, but also has adversely affected the morale and 
motivation of soldiers, their families and NOKs of martyrs? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) and (b) A 
distinction has been made by the Government between casualties in war and those 
arising out of border skirmishes and action against militants/terrorists/extremists etc., 
owing to the different levels of risk, the intensity of action involved in each case and also in 
the interest of the morale of the Armed Forces personnel. 
90 

[21 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
According to this policy, Operation Vijay was treated as a war-like 
engagement and a special welfare package including enhanced ex-gratia 
compensation of Rs. 10 lakhs to the Next of Kin of the Battle casualties was 
provided. However, no distinction has been made between Operation Vijay and 
post-Operation Vijay casualties, in so far as the pensionary benefits are 
concerned. All war widows would be entitled to liberalized family pension.

Submarine deal with France 
3079. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SI RIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has signed a US$ 1.8 billion submarine deal 
with France recently to acquire si x submarines to replace to "fast 
decommissioning" of India's fleet; 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
(b) the reasons for Government going in for a single tender and why did it not look 
at the two other contenders viz. German HDW and Russian Amur class submarines; 
and 
(c) additional benefits that the French Government is giving in this deal when 
compared to other two companies? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) to 
(c) Contracts for the indigenous construction of six French scorpene class submarines 
at Mazagon Dock Limited (MDL), Mumbai, were signed on 6th October 2005. The 
total cost of the project sanctioned by the Government is Rs. 18798 crore including 
Rs. 3553 crore as taxes. The project cost is inclusive of Rs. 2160 crore provided as 
budgetary estimate for Torpedo, protable Deep Water Noise Range, Base and Depot 
spares and MDL infrastructure. It also includes the cost of contract between MDL, 
Mumbai and M/s Armaris, France; MDL and Government of India; and 
Government of India and M/s MBDA, France. 
In 1997, the Government approved construction of two submarines at M/s MDL, 
Mumbai Though the request for proposals were sent to four firm, viz. M/s Thomas 
CSF, France, VSEL (UK), M/s Kockums (Sweden) and RVZ, Russia, only M/s 
Thomson CSF, France responded. M/s HDW, Germany was not considered as CBI was 
investigating certain allegations against the firm. Price negotiations were held 
with M/s Thomson CSF, France. However, no contract could be signed due to 
reluctance of the French Government to release missiles for the submarines and 
inadequate explanation of the cost of programme and logistic package. Thereafter, 
the Government decided to approve the proposal for the indigenous construction of 
six scorpene submarines under Transfer of Technology. 
In 1999, Government approved long term perspective plan for construction of 
24 submarines and acquisition of national competence in submarine building. Out of 
the 12 submarines to be constructed in phase 1, six are to be of western origin while 
the other six would be of Amur or other apropriate class. Russian Amur class 
submarines were not considered as the same were not envisaged for induction under the 
proposed production line. 
The transfer of the build technology of the Scorpene submarines would enable the 
Indian Navy to undertake modifications and replacement of equipment from third 
submarine onwards.

Bongaigaon Thermal Power Station 
3150. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the NTPC has totally disagreed to take over the 
Bongaigaon Thermal Power Station (BTPS), Assam and no policy to revive the same 
is undertaken by Government; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that no such policy was finalized to install new power 
project at the same place during the recent meeting of Chief Minister of Assam and Prime 
Minister as appeared in the print media; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING AND MINISTER 
OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS (SHRI PRIYARANJAN DASMUNSI): (a) 
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) has carried out a study for 
Renovation and Modernization (R&M) of Bongaigaon Thermal Power Station 
(BTPS) and found that though it is technically feasible to renovate the existing units of 
BTPS and found that though it is technically feasible to renovate the existing units of BTS, 
it would not be economically viable as the tariff works out to about Rs. 3.16 per unit 
after carrying out R&M at the estimated cost of Rs. 700 crores. Hence, capital 
grant/viability gap funding of Rs. 350 crores would have to be provided to bring down 
the tariff to an acceptable level of Rs. 2.50 per unit. Therefore, it was felt that it would be 
uneconomical to revive the existing power plant. 
(b) and (c) the proposal for installation of a new power project at the same place was 
discussed at the appropriate level of Government of India and it was decided that NTPC 
would set up a new 500 MW (2x250 MW) thermal power station at Bongaigaon, Assam at 
the existing location of Bongaigaon TPS. The power plant will be based on Flue Gas 
Desulphurisation (FGD) technology to enable it to use Assam coal.

Project units on account of high silt in the river Sutlej is approximately Rs.

It is not established that rapid deglaciation in Satluj catchment area in China 
is responsible for the unexpected behaviour of the river. However, with the 
formation of an artificial lake due to massive land slides at Pareechu in Tibet 
(China) in the year 2004-05 and its bursting in the year 2005-06 silt contents 
much higher than normal have been experienced in the river waters. Due to 
the flash flood on 26.6.2005, on account of bursting of the Pareechu artificial 
dam/lake, erosion was also caused to the upstream banks of the river Satluj 
which resulted in higher siltation of the river waters for some more time.

Water Resources with the Government of China in 2005 for supply of 
hydrological information in flood season beginning on-set of South West 
monsoon 2006.

†3159. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention have been drawn to wards news-item 
published under the caption "Sankatgrast Rajyon Ko Mahangi Bijli Bechne 
Valon Ke Khilaf Muhim"; 
(b) if so, the tariff at which power was sold to power scarce States by power 
surplus States during last three years; 
(c) the action, if any, taken by Government in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the impact thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING AND 
MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (d) As per the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003 the tariff 
for supply of electricity by the generation company to distribution licensee is to be 
determined by the Appropriate Electricity Regulatory Commission. In case such tariff 
has been determined through transparent process of bidding in accordance with the 
guidelines issued by the Central Government, the Electricity Regulatory Commissbn 
is required to adopt the tariff so determined. 
According to Section 86 of the Ac t, concerned St ate Electricity 
Regulatory Commission is required to regulate electricity purchase and 
procurement process of distribution licensee including the price at which 
electricity shall be procured from the generating companies or licensees or from 
other sources. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
Trading of electricity i.e., purchase of electricity for resale thereof, is a licensed 
activity under the provisions of the Act and licence to undertake trading is granted by the 
Appropriate Electricity Regulatory Commission. Concerned regulatory commission has 
powers under the Act to fix the trading margin, if considered necessary. Further, 
an Appropriate Commission has powers to issue such directions under Section 60 of 
the Act as it considers appropriate to a licensee or a generating company if such licensee or 
generating company enters into an agreement or abuses its dominant position or enters 
into a combination which is likely to cause or causes an adverse effect on competition of 
electricity industry. Non-compliance of the directions of the Commission is punishable under 
the Act. 
The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission has issued draft regulation 
seeking to fix trading margin.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) The 
National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 is applicable in rural areas of the 
country. The Act guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment in every financial 
year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual 
work. It is not restricted to the people living below poverty line. 
(c) The responsibilities of the Gram Panchayats have been given in Section 16

(i) The Gram Panchayat shall be responsible for identification of the projects in

recommendations of the Gram Sabha and the Ward Sabhas and for 
executing and supervising such works.

area of the Gram Panchayat as may be sanctioned by the Programme 
Officer. 
(iii) Every Gram Panchayat shall, after considering the recommendations 
of the Gram Sabha and the Ward Sabhas, prepare a development plan and 
maintain a shelf of possible works to be taken up under the Scheme as and 
when demand for work arises. 
(iv) The Gram Panchayat shall forward its proposals for the development 
projects including the order of priority between works to the Programme 
Officer for scrutiny and preliminary approval prior to the commencement 
of the year in which it is proposed to be executed.

†3188. SHRI LAXMINARAYAN SHARMA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

are having less than one acre of land; 
(b) whether Government propose to enhance the financial support to rural farmers 
owing meagre agricultural land and who have been rendered financially miserable 
due to flood, drought and other calamities; 
(c) whether almost all developed countries provide financial support of around 350 
billion dollars, the financial support provided to the farmer since the last three years in 
India; and 
(d) the measures taken by Government to see that agricultural vocation become 
beneficial? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) As per Report No. 472 of the National 
Sample Survey, 55th Round, about 71.72 percentage of persons possess less than 
one acre of land. 
(b) to (d): The State Governments are primarily responsible for undertaking 
necessary relief and rehabilitation measures in the areas affected by natural calamities 
out of the corpus of the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF), which is contributed by the 
Government of India and the State Government in the ratio of 3:1. In the event of 
calamity of a severe nature, in which the requirement of funds is beyond the funds 
available in the State CRF account, additional assistance is provided from national 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) after following the laid down procedure. 
Ministry of Home Affairs has laid down the norms and items to be covered for expenditure 
from CRF/NCCF. The assistance extended from the NCCF for droughts in the last three 
years is under: -

tariff peaks, tariff escalations and high  tariffs are being addressed through

Trade Organisation (WTO) in respect of import of Textiles and apparels in the 
developed countries including USA.

Karbi Anglong district in Assam, along with neighbouring North Cachar Hills district are 
two districts, which have majority of hill tribes in Assam. These districts have population of 
dominants tribes, namely, Karbis in Karbi Anglong and Dimasas in N.C. Hills. In both 
the districts, other tribes like Kukis, Hmars and Khasis are also settled in Sizeable numbers. 
Both the districts are covered under Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India and enjoy a 
large degree of autonomy. There have been tensions and rivalries between different tribes. 
During October 2003 to June 2004, there were clashes in Karbi Anglong between Karbis 
and Kukis over ginger cultivation. Clashes this year started with killing of three Dimasas in 
Diphu Policy Station area on 26th September, 2005. The situation took a communal turn 
and five Karbis were killed on 2nd October, 2005. There were incidents like attacks and 
burning of houses of the two communities. In a major violent incident, on 17th October, 
2005, forty Karbis were taken out of a bus and brutally killed. 
A large number of persons, who took shelter in the relief camps, have returned to their 
native places. At present (as on 13th November, 2005) about 19,500 people are in relief 
camps in Karbi Anglong, Nagaon and N.C. Hills districts. Rehabilitation measures 
undertaken by the State include sanction of Rs. 3 lakhs as ex-gratia grant to the next of the 
kin of the victims; providing Gratuitous Relief (GR) to the affected families; and, 
rehabilitation assistance for construction of houses. The Government of India is 
helping the Government of Assam for granting ex-gratia to the deceased family, 
providing GR and rehabilitation grant to the affected families. 
The violent activities in Karbi Anglong suspected to have been abetted by the militant 
groups of the particular tribes for area domination. 
Shri Sriprakash Jaiswal, the Minister of State, in the Ministry of Home Affairs, visited 
Karbi Anglong on 20th October, 2005, and met the people affected by the violence. The 
Secretary (Border management), in the Ministry of Home Affairs, also visited Diphu at the 
same time and reviewed the security situation with the Chief Secretary, GDP and other 
security forces. A senior officer from the Ministry, again, visited Diphu on 4th 
November, 2005, and reviewed the security situation and rehabilitation process. Additional 
Central Police Forces and Army were also deployed to help the State Government to 
control the situation.

The Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Sir, I move:- 
"That the Bill further to amend the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, as passed by 
Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, I will take only a couple of minutes to introduce this Bill. 
Sir, the Central Sales Tax is a tax levied on inter-State sale of goods and is collected 
by the State Government. Now, against the orders of the Assessing Officers, appeals 
are provided. In 2001, 2002 and 2003, the Act was amended to provide for an appellate 
authority at the Centre. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI) in the chair. Unfortunately, 
while amending the Act, appeal was provided against the orders of an assessing authority. 
Now, the intention was not to provide for appeal in Delhi against the order of every 
assessing authority in every

State. The intention was that this should be the final appellate authority. Therefore, when 
the practical problem was pointed out, we are now amending the Act to correct the 
error that was committed in 2001 and 2002. The appeal now to the Central Appellate 
Authority will be against the order of the final appellate authority in the State so that 
millions of appeals don't land up here. 
Secondly, Sir, we are not creating a separate tribunal. We are requesting, or, by 
this Act authorising the Advanced Tax Ruling Authority under the Income-tax Act to also 
function as the Central Sales Tax Appellate Authority. The reason is obvious. The 
Central Sales Tax is proposed to be phased out in, two or three years. There is no need 
to create a separate tribunal and appoint separate judges for that and create an 
infrastructure. Therefore, we are taking steps to name this authority as the appellate 
authority. The Central Sales Tax, I believe, we are under discussions with the State Finance 
Ministers' Empowered Committe, will be phased out in two years or so, may be, in three 
years or so. Once that decision is taken, the CST will go. Sir, this is an interim arrangement. I 
request that the House may kindly be pleased to return the Bill.

Concern over miseries faced by Haj pilgrims from Kerala due to certain 
actions of Air India 
SHRI M.P. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Sir, this is to draw the attention of 
the House to the pathetic way of Air India dealing with the passengers from Kerala. 
Even Haj pilgrims are put to trouble by disorders on the part of Air India. All of a sudden 
flights were cancelled or time schedule was changed. This naturally led to various 
miseries and the pilgrims had to suffer severely. Sometimes aircrafts with small number 
of seats were sent to Calicut to take the pilgrims. This was equal to denying travel of 
good number of pilgrims same day. With the timely intervention and help of the Minister 
of State for External Affairs and the care of the Haj Committee, the situation was set right. 
Later the Air India arranged additional flights to Calicut. But this cannot undo the difficulties 
already faced by the passengers. Sir, technical snag has become a permanent 
justification for this kind of negative approach towards passengers. This cannot be a 
shield to cover cruel delays of flight departure and cancellation of flight itself. And, Air 
India effects unjustifiable increase in air fare, especially on the Gulf routes. From 
Trivandrum, for example, air fare to Dubai, in economy class, is Rs. 16,050, while 
it is only Rs. 13,800 from Mumbai. The ticket charge of the Haj Pilgrims who travel with 
private tour operators also was suddenly increased. There is a widespread protest 
among the people of Kerala against this exploitation of the citizens a large majority of 
whom are poor employees and they travel to the Gulf to eke out their livelihood. The air fare 
for Haj pilgrims is also higher than the ordinary charge on the same route. The national 
carrier should show mercy towards Keralites, whose contribution forms a large portion of 
Air India's income. Hence, I urge upon the Government to take steps to protect the 
customers' rights of the people of India. Thank you.

SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, my Special Mention is pertaining to the need to

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
I wish to urge upon the Government the pressing need to launch more 
schemes to provide soft loans to farmers and the poor people in the rural as well 
as urban areas. The loan distribution target of the banks in the country for the 
year 2005-2006, is Rs, 22,036 crores. Out of this Rs. 12,345 crores is allocated for 
agricultural sector. Though this is more than the allocation for agriculture sector 
last year, there is a need to double this allocation. As agriculture is subjected to 
the vagaries of nature, farmers' future is uncertain. We all know how badly 
farmers have been hit in Tamil Nadu in the recent rains and floods, that is why it is 
necessary to provide soft loans to farmers. Such a step will also increase the 
agricultural production and safeguard the food security of the country. In the 
same way, the urban and rural poor, who are dependent on other avocations, 
should also be given soft loans in order to eradicate poverty. The hon. Chief 
Minister of Tamil Nadu has demanded for increasing the ratio of bank share to 
3 percent. Now, the banks give loans under Women Self-Help Group Scheme in 
the ratio of 1:1.3. That is, if the rotational fund of Self-Help Group is Rs. 1000, the 
banks give Rs. 1300 as loan. This should be increased to Rs. 3000 immediately. 
Such a step will encourage the saving habit among people and will be very 
useful to the poor. In Tamil Nadu 3.5 lakh people of Self-Help Groups are being 
benefited due to the initiatives taken by Tamil Nadu Government. So, I appeal to 
the Centre to launch new loan schemes for the farmers and the poor. Thank you.

displaced due to formation of national parks and

SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Sir, in my home State Karnataka, 201

these families could not be rehabilitated due to paucity of funds by the State Government

Central assistance of Rs. 18.35 crores so as to rehabilitate these families. 
Similarly, 154 tribal families were displaced due to the formation of Bandipur 
National Park. As per the norms prescribed by the Central Government each displaced 
family has to be given one lakh rupees as compensation. A sum of Rs. 77 lakhs was 
released in 2004-05 by the Central Government for which the State Government 
has already furnished the utilisation certificate. The Central Government is yet to 
release the balance amount of Rs. 77 lakhs so as to give the prescribed compensation 
to the families. 
Similarly, Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary was formed on the condition that the 
Government of India would provide 100 per cent financial assistance to Karnataka 
for acquisition of land for the sanctuary and the State was to bear the entire cost of 
rehabilitation. The Central Government is yet to release the balance amount of Rs. 
132 lakhs to the State Government. 
Thus the Central Government has to release a total sum of Rs. 20.44 
crores to the State Government of Karnataka for the rehabilitation of families 
affected due to formation of Kudremukh National Park, Bandipur National Park and 
the cost of land of Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary. I, therefore, demand that the Central 
Government should release Rs. 20.44 crores to Karnataka on priority basis for the 
said purposes.

Demand for Providing Professional Skills to Workforce in the 
Country 
SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, India has a workforce of 
around 400 million, but only about 5 per cent of them in the age group of 20-24 
have obtained vocational skills through formal training system. The lack of 
professional skills among the educated is considered to be one of the major 
factors for large unemployment. This is because our education system is 
excessively oriented towards general academic education with a little or no 
vocational orientation. About 9 per cent  of the workforce is engaged in the 
unorganised sector. Major concern in India is that a large number of persons 
engaged in the unorganised sector are working with low level of productivity 
and income. Out of an estimated 397 million people employed in the 
unorganised sector, about 122 million people are living below the poverty line. 
In this regard, the World Employment Report has indicated that in the present 
context of globalisation, demand for unskilled and under-skilled labourers has 
declined while the demand for skilled and multi-skilled labour has increased. 
The Expert Group headed by Dr. B.N. Gupta also recomm ended introduction 
of multi-skilling courses in ITIs and identified new areas covering agriculture 
sector for starting training in agro-related trades. As the first step, the 
Government should upgrade the existing 1986 Government-run ITIs. The 
upgraded ITIs should function as Centres of Excellence for producing multi-
skilled workforce of international stand ard. The Government should also set 
up, at least, 1000 more off-campus centres in the country to train under-skilled 
labourers, so that the poor also reap the benefit of globalisation.

Demand for recognition of 'Kannada' as a Classical Language 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka):  Sir, I would like to draw the 
attention of the Government to the need  recognising 'Kannada' as a classical 
language. 
On the occasion of the Golden Jubilee of the unified State of Karnataka, it would 
be a benefitting gesture on the part of the Centre to commemorate the event 
with a declaration of granting the Classic al Language status to Kannada for 
which it eminently qualifies under the criteria set forth by the Centre in this 
regard. 
'Kannada' has deep roots, being a member of the Dravidian family of 
languages with an antiguity of more than 2000 years, with a recorded history 
of over 1000 years. Its literary output, both quantitative and qualitative, is 
unique and distinct, and is not borrowed or influenced by any other classical 
language. The UNESCO Document on As ia Scripts recognises the 'Kannada' 
script as one of the major scripts in the world. 
'Kannada' scores on all four benchmarks that a classical language should

Need to provided nutritious food to children of Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO( Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my Special Mention 
pertains to severe malnutrition in Children of Andhra Pradesh — Need to take 
measures to provide nutritious food. 
Sir, one of the promises made in the NCMP is that a comprehensive 
medium-term strategy for food and nutrition security would be worked out in 
three months. It is close to two years since the UPA came to power, but 
nothing has been done so far. The inaction of the Government of India is taking its 
toll in Andhra Pradesh. The people, especially, children are poorly nourished in 
Andhra Pradesh when compared with other States or even the national average. 
According to the Report of 2005 prepared by Andhra Pradesh Social Watch 
which is based on the figures from the rural food insecurities prepared by Dr. 
Swaminathan Foundation and the World Food Programme, 38 per cent men 
and 42 per cent women are suffering from chronic energy deficiency in 
villages, 10.5 per cent children are severely undernourished, and 28.2 per cent 
are moderately undernourished. Severe malnutrition leads to functional 
impairment. The average protein intake is 62 grams/calorie unit a day as 
against all India figure of 72. The study also points out that per capita 
consumption of food items is much below the norm set by the ICMR. The per 
capita consumption of pulses is 860 against national average of 960.; milk 
3.96 against 4.60; fruits 0.97 kgs, against 1.06 kgs. Consumption of food 
provides important information about the food security situation in any place. 
Looking at the situation, I request the Government of India to immediately 
begin fulfilment of its nutrition security promise in Andhra Pradesh. Otherwise, 
the people, especially, children in Andhra Pradesh will become  'nutritionally 
impaired".

term health problems, including distress, and make attempts at suicide. The

Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles. 
The Constitution not only grants equality to women, but also empowers the State 
to adopt positive measures in favour of women. The same thing has been said in 
the National Policy for the Empowernment of Women. But, these are words, which 
only sound good, since we lack in implementing them in letter and spirit. 
Sir, I have a few suggestions to make  for the consideration of the hon. 
Minister. I don't want to dwell upon the increasing number of rape cases, 
particularly in North India, the incident s last year in Manipur involving the 
Armed Forces, or the latest incident in which a woman's hands were chopped 
off. Many hon. Members have mentioned these things. 
Sir, my first point is about domestic violence. Domestic violence is violence 
against love, violence against humanity, physical battering, intimidation, 
spousal neglect and a prison in which a woman is trapped into submission. 
Despite the apparent neutrality of the term, domestic

violence is always a gender-specific crime, perpetrated by men against women. 
Domestic violence is perpetrated not only by the husband, but also by the in-
laws and others. All are violations of the most fundamental human rights of 
women. 
The violence against women cuts across boundaries, religions, cultures 
and income groups. Even according to the UNESCO study, 45 per cent of 
Indian women are slapped, kicked or b eaten by their husbands. India is also 
having the highest rate of violence during pregnancy. If we consider women-
related violence, 50 per cent women are kicked, beaten or hit when pregnant, 
and 78.4 per cent of the women wo suffered violence have attempted committing 
suicide. This year, we had passed Domestic Violence Bill without any discussion. 
Sir, according to UNESCO 'psychological abuse' is also a domestic violence. 
But, nothing has been mentioned about this even in the Bill that we passed. 
And, Sir. there is a clear cut difference between 'emotional abuse' and 
'psychological abouse.' 'Emotional abuse' is an affective state of 
consciousness in which joy, sorrow, fe ar, hate, etc., is experienced. But, 
'psychological abuse' is affecting the state of mind. So, I appeal to the Minister 
to study this and make necessary changes to treat psychological abuse as one of 
the atrocities against women. 
The second point is, the Labour Ministry recently allowed women to work at 
night shifts also. And I need to tell the hon. Minister about the atrocious 
behaviour on women at workplace. We have umpteen such instances. But, 
there is no legislation to contain sexual abuse of women at workplace. So, I 
request that there is an urgent need to bring legislation to control sexual abuse at 
workplace. 
Sir, my third point is with regard to rape, which, to my mind, is the most 
dreadful act on women and is common in our country. Sir, rape is defined in 
India as intentional, unlawful sexual intercourse with a woman without her 
consent. The essential elements of this  definition under Section 375 of the 
Indian Penal Code are sexual intercourse with a woman and the absence of 
consent. This definition, therefore, does not include acts of forced oral sex, or 
sodomy, or penetration by foreign objects; instead, those actions are 
criminalized under section 354 of the IPC, which deals with criminal assault on a 
woman with intent to outrage

her modesty and Section 377 IPC, covering carnal intercourse against the order of 
nature. We have been demanding for inclusion of the above under Section 375 and to 
provide more stringent punishment. But, so far, nothing has been done. I request the 
hon. Minister to ponder over this and save the women in India. 
It is ridiculous that Section 155(4) of the Evidence Act takes into account the moral 
character of a victim of rape at the time of trial. How can a prosecutrix, who may be a 
poor woman or a tribal woman or an uneducated woman, prove that she has moral 
character. This kind of provisions further gives an elbowroom to males to get out of the 
clutches from law. So, I strongly feel that there is no meaning to this Section and this sub-
section should be deleted straightaway. 
With these words, I conclude. Thank you.

STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS 
Outcome of the negotiations at Sixth Ministerial Conference of World 
Trade Organisations held in Hong Kong, China from 13th to 18th 
December, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL NATH): 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, hon. Mem bers will recall that I had made a 
statement in this House on 7th December, 2005 on the Hong Kong Ministerial 
Conference of the Commerce and Trade Mi nisters of 149 member countries 
from 13—18 December, 2005. The Minister s issued a declaration, copies of 
which have been placed in the Parliament Library. 
During this Conference, India was proactive in articulating its position on 
issues of concern to us and other developing countries, especially in the 21 
member G-20 alliance and 45 member G-33 alliance. India played a key role in 
further strengthening the developing country coalitions by bringing together G-
20, G-33 and G-90 groups of countries in a Grand alliance to reinforce each 
other's position on issues of mutual interest. India also enabled the formation 
of NAMA 11 Group (countries such as India, Brazil, Argentina, South Africa, 
Philippines, Indonesia, etc.) to pursue and integrate meaningfully Special and 
Differential Treatment issues in Non-Agricultural Market Access matters. 
As far as India is concerned, the Hong Kong Ministerial Declaration finally 
agreed upon, addresses our core concerns and interests and provides us 
enough negotiating space for future work leading up to modalities. The text has 
positive development content, which would need to be built upon and fully 
realized in the next stage of negotiations. 
The Declaration stipulates that the negotiations must be concluded, by 2006 
and establishes time-lines and targets in specific areas. Among other issues, in 
Agriculture and NAMA, we agreed that the modalities are to be established by 
30 April 2006 and comprehensive draft schedules submitted by 31 July 2006. 
324 

[21 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The principal elements of t he text represent significant grains for India. In 
Agriculture, in Domestic Support, developing countries like India with no AMS 
(Aggregate Measurement of Support) commitments will be exempt from any 
cuts on their de minimis support. Green Box criteria will be reviewed so that 
programmes of developing country members which have minimal trade 
distorting effect will be incorporated into the Green Box. All forms of Export 
Subsidies by developed countries and other export measures with equivalent 
effect (such as Export Credits, guarantees & Insurance in excess of 180 days, 
and to trade distorting practices of STEs and Food Aid) will be eliminated by 
the end of 2013, with the substantial part eliminated by the middle of the 
implementation period I.e. 2010. Developing countries like India will continue to 
benefit from the provisions of Articl e 9.4 of the Agreement on Agriculture i.e. 
they shall be able to continue to provide marketing and transport subsidies for 5 
years after elimination of export subsidies, i.e. up to 2018. Developing 
countries will be able to self-designate an appropriate number of tariff lines as 
Special Products guided by indicators based on the criteria of food security, 
livelihood security and rural development. To safeguard our farmers against 
surge in imports or fall in international prices, developing countries will have 
recourse to a Special Safeguard Mechanism with both import quantity and 
price triggers. 
Specifically, on Cotton, export subsidies by developed countries will be fully 
eliminated in 2006; and trade distor ting domestic support by developed 
countries will be reduced ambitiously over a shorter period than for other 
agricultural products. 
On Non Agricultural Market Access (NAMA), the Declaration calls for a Swiss 
Formula with coefficients. This fo rmulations preserve the ABI formula 
submitted by Argentina, Brazil and India for multiple coefficients based on each 
country's tariff average. The Declaration reiterates that Special and Differential 
Treatment for developing countries be maintained through the principal of less than 
full reciprocity in reduction commitments and the flexibilities to exclude a certain 
percentage of tariff lines from tariff cuts. The Declaration also recognizes the 
sensitivity attached to the unbound tariff lines by providing for a non-linear 
mark up before applying formula reductions. It is agreed that tariff peaks, tariff 
escalations

RAJYA SABHA [21 December, 2005] 
and high tariffs on products of export interest to developing countries be either 
reduced or eliminated. It is also agreed that participation in the sectoral initiatives to 
reduce or eliminate tariffs will be on a non-mandatory basis. 
In Services, developing countries will have adequate policy space and 
necessary flexibility to pursue their developmental objectives. The primacy of 
the Request—offer process has been maintained. In Mode-1 and Mode-2 
(including Cross Border Supply), guidance for commitments at the existing 
levels has been secured. Members have agr eed to offer enhanced 
commitments in Mode-4 (Movement of Natural Persons). We agreed to removal 
or substantial reduction of the Economic Needs Test. This has been one of the 
principal barriers to export of Services from developing countries, and has 
been a longstanding demand of India. It was also agreed that the approaches to 
negotiations, which includes plurilateral negotiations, will follow the GATS 
Agreement and the Negotiating Guidelines and Procedures evolved in 2003. 
The Declaration does not introduce any compulsion on developing countries for 
opening up services sectors. Revised offers would be submitted by 31 July 
2006, and final draft schedules would be readied by 31 October 2006. 
The Declaration notes the amendm ent made a fortnight ago, s pearheaded 
by the Agrican Group and supported by India, to the TRIPS Agreements to 
incorporate the Public Health conc erns. On the Implementation Issues 
relating to TRIPS and the Convention on Biodiversity, and extension of the 
protection of Geographical Indications, the Declaration calls for intensification of 
consultations so that the General Council could take appropriate action by 31 
July 2006. 
India spoke not only for herself, but in the tradition established since the 
time of Pandit Jawahar Lal Nehru and Smt. Indira Gandhi, we also lent a 
powerful voice to the concerns of least developed countries. Through close 
co-ordination with the LDC Group and the Africa Group, we were instrumental 
in fashioning an LDC package. 
As part of Special and Differential Treatment, the Membership agreed to five 
LDC specific proposals, including the one relating to provision of duty-free and 
quota-fee market access in developed countries for products originating from 
LDCs. We further directed that on the remaining proposals, recommendations be 
made by December 2006.

The contours of the Domestic Support reduction formula in Agriculture as also the tariff 
reduction formulae in Agriculture as well as NAMA have been given shape. The coming 
months will see intense negotiations, as the modalities are finalized. The Government 
will continue its close engagement with various stakeholders in each of the areas, so that 
the best result could be obtained, fully protecting our farmers, industry, as well as 
promoting our national interests and core concerns.

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATH): Sir, the debate has 
been very emotional, and the hon. Members have made very good points. By and large 
they have not made any political points, but they have tried to understand the problem 
and suggest as to how this problem can be tackled. For this, they should be 
congratulated and thanked. 
One of the most important things, which should be borne in mind by all of us, is that in 
India women are respected, respected a great deal. Mother, daughter, sister, wife, all 
women are respected, and this is something which can, ultimately, help us also. But 
what is not done in India is also equally important. Women are respected, but they are 
not given the authority in the House, in the Government and in the society. They are 
respected; but they are not empowered. And, since the beginning, the struggle is 
going on for empowering the women --empowering the women economically, 
empowering the women socially and empowering the women politically. The struggle is 
going on, and the members of the same family sometimes are on the opposite side. The 
men are on the one side and the women are on the other side when the question of 
empowerment is taken up. It is very interesting to note that when for the first time the 
Sharada Bill was introduced, a lot of very enlightened souls opposed it. What did the 
Sharada Act propose? The Sharada Act proposed that women should have a right to 
divorce; that was socially empowering the women. Women should have a right 
376 

[21 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to own the property. It is very interesting to know that before the Hindu Succession Act 
was enacted, the women were allowed to purchase the property, but they were allowed to 
own the property. 
Before that, women were not allowed even to possess the property, leave aside own 
the property. So, the Hindu Succession Act provided that women should be given the 
right to own and possess property. That was economically empowering the women. 
Afterwards, during the period of Shri Rajiv Gandhi's premiership, women were politically 
empowered. It was found that they were not able to come to local bodies, or, get 
elected to local bodies easily. That is why, it was provided by amending the Constitution 
that they would have 33 per cent seats reserved for them in Zilla Parishads, Panchayat 
Samitis, in corporations and in Gram Panchayats. And 33 per cent seats were given to 
them. That was politically empowering them. Now, we are considering as to how they 
can be empowered to have their legislative right and come to the State Legislatures and 
the Parliament. This is how the things have moved. They were respected, but they were 
not given authority or empowered. They were not given the authority. This is the 
difference, sir. Respect was given; but the authority was not given. This made a lot of 
difference to the lives of women in the country. That has to be very clearly 
understood. Whenever we are discussing issues of this nature, it is good to forget to 
which party we belong and try to understand the nature of the problem and try to suggest 
real solutions which can be had, so that if the problem is not entirely done away with, at 
least, it is reduced in its severity and some kind of relief is given. That should be our 
attitude and, fortunately, that has been the attitude of the Members in the House. 
Sir, while discussing this issue, many cases were brought to the notice of this House. 
We will certainly remember those cases and try to give relief to the people who are 
really affected. But, ,it is not possible to come to correct conclusions by concentrating 
upon few separated, individual, cases as such. We shall have to take the totality 
into consideration. 
Now, very Member in the House said that offences against women had increased. 
Yes, they have increased. But we shall have to understand in what fashion they have 
increased. In 1997, the total number of offences committed against women were 1,21,265. In 
2004, this number has gone

are more cases. Maybe, they are not registered and they are not noted. There 
are bound to be cases. But in the number of cases which are with us, in 1997 
and in 2004 -- it is a period of eight years - how much is the increase? The 
increase is that of nearly 35,000 cases. How much is the increase in population? 
It is nearly ten crores. The increase in the number of cases is nearly 35,000. 
We are sorry that the number has not declined. We are sorry that this is

gets reduced. Yet, to put the case in a proper perspective, I would like to say 
that these are the figures. So let us not come to the conclusion that the

but when you look at this number against the background of the increase in 
population, which is equal to ten cases of people, probably, we can say that we, 
as a whole, not the Government or the Police - I am not talking about the 
Government and the Police because this cannot be done only by the 
Government and the Police... The entir e society, others, the families, 
educational institutions, all have to contribute, and they have contributed. Now, 
this fact I would like to submit to this House very humbly, Sir. 
Sir, the second point which I would like to put before this House relates to the 
persons who are responsible for committing this offence. Who commits this 
offence? Who is committing this offence? Sir, the analysis is very interesting. 
The offences against women are committed by their relatives more than the 
unknown persons. The offences against women are committed by the persons 
who are their employers; the offences  against women are committed by their 
own friends. There are some persons who are unconnected, unrelated and they 
also are responsible for this. But, if you analyse these facts, you will come to 
know that the offences are committed by those who are near and close to 
women themselves, their family members. It is a very interesting thing. Shri -
Pachouriji referred to that figure. It is a very interesting thing. I am giving the 
figures of 2004, and the figures of 2004 indicate that 1,53,333 offences were 
committed. Out of this number, 58,1 21 offences were committed by the 
husbands and relatives against women. One-thirds of the offences were 
committed by their relatives, by the husbands and their relatives. Now, the saas
